marketing-analysis.name: Marketing Analysis Pack
marketing-analysis.intro: Pages for analyzing markets, customers, and campaign effectiveness. Formats range from strategy (SWOT / 3C / TAM-SAM-SOM / positioning) through customer understanding (RFM / cohort), behavior (funnel), to effect verification (A/B testing) — one page per format.
marketing-analysis.short: Pages for analyzing markets, customers, and campaign effectiveness

b2b-sales.name: B2B Sales Pack
b2b-sales.intro: Pages that visualize a deal's stakeholder structure and discovery (issue exploration). Each page shares, on one slide, who influences the decision and what has not yet been learned.
b2b-sales.short: Pages that visualize deal stakeholder structure and discovery (issue exploration)

scalar-ae.name: Scalar AE Pack
scalar-ae.intro: Standard pages that Scalar account executives use for deal reviews and activity plans. Designed so the contents of account.json (the deal ledger) can be poured in directly. The only stable pack.
scalar-ae.short: Standard pages Scalar account executives use for deal reviews and activity plans

planning.name: Planning Pack
planning.intro: Pages that present time-based plans. The three formats — Gantt chart, chronology, and milestone timeline — differ in granularity and use case.

analysis.name: Current-State Analysis Pack
analysis.intro: Pages built from consulting current-state analysis and issue-identification frameworks. Covers structural decomposition (logic tree / KPI tree), root cause (why-why / fishbone diagram), quantitative narrowing (Pareto chart), gap and process flow, external environment (PEST / Five Forces), and prioritization. Used by the current-state-analysis skill.
analysis.short: Pages built from consulting current-state analysis and issue-identification frameworks

read-alone.name: Read-Alone Pack
read-alone.intro: Pages of high-density slides that can be read to completion on a single page (consulting-firm-style handouts). Each fits a governing message, lead-in, evidence, implication, and source onto one slide. Every template carries $density variants, so the same file renders at two densities: print (handout) and presentation (stage).
read-alone.short: Pages of high-density slides that can be read to completion on a single page

swot-analysis.description: Organizes internal and external environment into four positive/negative quadrants and shows priority actions
swot-analysis.answers: What are our strategic strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats?
guardrails: Distinguish between facts and interpretations
Do not assert causal relationships based on SWOT wording alone

three-c-analysis.description: Shows the strategic focus arising from the overlap of Customer, Competitor, and Company
three-c-analysis.answers: Where is the strategic territory where customer value and competitive advantage overlap?

market-sizing.description: Shows the total market down to the obtainable market as nested circles
market-sizing.answers: How large is the market, and what is the realistic obtainable range?

positioning-map.description: Shows the positional relationship between us and competitors on two axes
positioning-map.answers: Are we delivering value that differs from competitors?

rfm-segments.description: Compares customer segments and measures based on purchase recency, frequency, and monetary value
rfm-segments.answers: Who are the loyal, developing, and dormant customers, and which measures should be applied to each?

cohort-retention.description: Compares retention rates by acquisition cohort across periods
cohort-retention.answers: Is the retention rate of newly acquired customers improving?
guardrails: Do not naively compare bottom-right cells that cover different observation periods
Note cohorts with small sample sizes

conversion-funnel.description: Shows counts at each stage of the purchase process and the biggest drop-off point
conversion-funnel.answers: Which stage's drop-off should be prioritized for improvement?

experiment-result.description: Shows control and treatment group results, sample sizes, the difference, and the verdict on a single page
experiment-result.answers: How much did the key KPI change as a result of the measure?
guardrails: Do not conclude that a non-significant result means zero effect
State the pre-defined primary KPI and analysis period

influence-map.description: Places buying-committee members on two axes — influence and stance — to show whom to move to win the deal
influence-map.answers: Whom do we need to move to close this deal, and is influence skewed toward the opposing side?
guardrails: Base positions on statements confirmed in meetings. Do not place sales' own hopes as if they were the stakeholder's stance
Do not place uncontacted stakeholders as "neutral." Put unknowns into discovery-gaps instead
Base influence on whether the person actually mattered in past approvals, not on job title
Keep bubble labels to 6 characters or fewer. Put job-title and name details in buying-committee instead

Bubbles are 0.95in in diameter. If placed too close together, labels get hidden (the --dry-run figure audit stops on "Text is hidden behind a shape drawn later"). Merge stakeholders that appear at the same position, or split them out into buying-committee

buying-committee.description: Lists each buying-committee member's role, influence, stance, and contact status
buying-committee.answers: Who is involved in the purchase, and how much access have we gained so far?
guardrails: Write the buying role as the function this person serves in this deal (approver, champion, evaluator, user, gatekeeper, opponent), not their job title
Write contact status based on actual meetings held. Do not count a mere business-card exchange as "contacted"

decision-structure.description: Shows, as a tree, which path an approval request follows and where it could stall
decision-structure.answers: In what order does approval move up, and where might it stop?
guardrails: Draw this deal's approval route, not the org chart. Do not include departments that are not involved
If the route changes depending on the amount, state in the source line that this is the route for the assumed amount
Depth of 4 or more, or more than 8 leaves, causes text to become crushed. Split by department

discovery-map.description: Lists the items to confirm during the deal and color-codes each as confirmed, hypothesis, or unconfirmed
discovery-map.answers: What do we know in this deal, and what is still just a hypothesis?
guardrails: State is one of three values: confirmed (verified by the customer's statement or a document), wip (partially confirmed), or missing (unconfirmed)
Do not mark sales' own guesses as confirmed. Anything whose corroborating source cannot be named is wip or lower
Do not move on to drafting the proposal while red (missing) items remain

pain-chain.description: Traces how a frontline problem cascades into departmental and executive metrics
pain-chain.answers: Which executive-level number is the frontline issue actually affecting?
guardrails: A chain link is a causal claim. Do not connect two stages with an arrow unless each stage has supporting evidence
Describe the impact on executive metrics using the customer's own numbers. If it's our own estimate, label it clearly as an estimate
Do not present correlation as causation

discovery-gaps.description: Breaks down the open questions that remain blank into who will confirm them and by when
discovery-gaps.answers: Whom do we need to ask what, next, to move the deal forward?
guardrails: Do not ask about an item if you cannot state why it matters. What decides success is the order of questions, not the quantity
Do not leave a row without a person to confirm with and a deadline
Keep this aligned one-to-one with the missing / wip items in discovery-map

influence-map-org.description: Arranges buying-committee members by organizational connections, showing role, influence, stance, and meeting status
influence-map-org.answers: Who reports to whom, and where is influence and support concentrated?
guardrails: The contents of people / links are validated by scripts/account_graph.py. Duplicate ids, dangling reportsTo references, and cycles are caught there, so always pass data that has gone through account_graph.load()
If there are more than 9 people, thin them out with account_graph.extract() and write "see the draw.io version for the other N people" in more. Do not cram everyone onto one slide
Include unmet stakeholders with met: false (drawn as a dashed line). Not having met someone is itself information
Base stance on statements made in meetings. Do not write sales' own hopes into stance

discovery-map-tree.description: Connects Goal, Strategy, and Tactics by support relationships, showing what supports what
discovery-map-tree.answers: What supports the customer's goal, and where do we make a difference?
guardrails: The contents of nodes / edges are validated by scripts/account_graph.py. Cycles and downward-pointing edges are caught there, so always pass data that has gone through account_graph.load()
The tier is determined by graph depth, not by a tier field. A lower-level goal that supports a higher-level goal is placed one level below it
If there are more than 9 nodes, thin them out with account_graph.extract() and write "see the draw.io version for the other N items" in more
Do not place a goal in Goal that the customer never stated. Treat guesses as wip items in the discovery map instead

account-snapshot.description: Shows, on one page, what stage this deal is in now, the amount, and when it will close
account-snapshot.answers: Where does this deal stand right now, for how much, and when will it close?
guardrails: forecast is one of four values: Pipeline / Best / Commit / Closed. Demote a Commit to Best if you cannot state its basis
Write an amount only if you can state how it was calculated. If you cannot, write "undetermined"
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

phase-gate.description: Lists the current stage's exit criteria and judges each by whether customer-side evidence has been obtained
phase-gate.answers: What customer-side evidence shows that the current stage's exit criteria are met?
guardrails: State is one of three values: met / partial / unmet. "We explained it" or "we sent the proposal" does not count as grounds for met
Evidence must come from the customer side (statements, documents, approval records). Internal agreement is not evidence
Map each exit criterion to a gate ID in references/scalar/sales-playbook.md §2
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

bant-risk.description: Identifies which of Budget / Authority / Needs / Timeframe is most likely to stall the deal
bant-risk.answers: Where is the risk in this deal, and is the forecast reasonable?
guardrails: Fix the order of the four items as Budget → Authority → Needs → Timeframe
Open each item with ok / risk / unknown, and write the basis for that judgment in the same cell
Send any item still marked unknown to action-plan with a person to confirm with and a deadline
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

action-plan.description: Breaks each unconfirmed issue down into who, asks whom, by when, and what completion looks like
action-plan.answers: To move this deal forward, who does what, by when?
guardrails: Do not include a row whose completion criterion cannot be written. "Confirm it" is not a completion criterion
Do not leave a row without a deadline. If the counterpart is internal, name the meeting body (WPS / Deal Desk)
Map each row one-to-one to an unconfirmed item in discovery-gaps
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

activity-timeline.description: Lists, in chronological order, who we've met and what we learned
activity-timeline.answers: How much access have we gained with this customer, and what have we learned?
guardrails: Limit the table to the most recent 4 entries. Keep earlier history in the ledger (account.json); do not put it on the slide
Write only the customer's own statements or documents under "what we learned." Do not write our own impressions
Do not omit dates, so gaps where we had no contact remain visible
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

visit-plan.description: Decides, before the visit, what to get out of it, how to ask, and how to respond
visit-plan.answers: What do we want to get from the customer on this visit, and how will we respond to expected objections?
guardrails: Make the title "the one thing we want to hear from the customer." "Explain X" is not an objective
Always state in ask which person or department we want introduced next, and why
Frame questions so the answer isn't just Yes/No (include SPIN's Implication and Need-payoff questions)
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

win-plan.description: A one-page summary of the win strategy and risks used to decide stage advancement and proposal investment in WPS
win-plan.answers: Why can we win this deal, and how will we neutralize the biggest risk?
guardrails: Write in resolution why the customer would choose us, not a list of product names
Pair each risk with a next action we can control. Anything without an actionable next step is capped at Best
Always accompany this with a verbal request for a continue / hold / withdraw decision
Internal document. Do not share with customers or partners (it includes individuals' influence, stance, and internal politics)

challenge-hypothesis.description: A one-pager that surfaces issues the customer hasn't yet articulated, to open a dialogue
challenge-hypothesis.answers: What issue has the customer not yet noticed, and what happens if it's left unaddressed?
guardrails: **For customer presentation**. Do not write about individuals' influence, stance, internal politics, or competitors' weaknesses
Fix the three cards in the order: groundwork → reframing → evidence (cost of inaction)
Do not assert as fact. Phrase hypotheses so they read as hypotheses, and always end with a question to the customer
Do not include figures without a source. Cite the source for any public case study

gantt-schedule.description: A period-by-task bar chart showing work streams running in parallel and their milestones
gantt-schedule.answers: When does what run in parallel, and when is the next milestone?
guardrails: Start and end are decimals in column units (0 is the left edge of the first column, the column count is the right edge). Values exceeding the column count raise an error at generation time
A row where start == end is drawn as a milestone (◆). Give a row width if you want it drawn as a bar
Dependency arrows are not represented. If you need to show fine-grained sequencing, write it as a table instead
Limit to 8 rows. Bundle fine-grained tasks so each row is one workstream
Do not mix planned values with actuals. For a planned schedule, state the planning date in source

chronology.description: A vertical chronology of dates and events showing how we arrived at the current state
chronology.answers: What has happened so far, and what sequence of events led to the current state?
guardrails: Write only facts in the event column. Keep interpretation and evaluation separate, in "implications"
Keep the date granularity consistent (all years, or all year-months, not mixed)
Limit to 9 rows. Bundle earlier history or narrow the period covered
If a quiet period is meaningful, don't omit the row — write "no change" to show it explicitly

milestone-timeline.description: Arranges milestones at equal intervals along a single horizontal timeline, showing the next decision point
milestone-timeline.answers: How are the milestones arranged, and when is the next point we need to act?
guardrails: Limit to 6 milestones. The timeline is drawn at equal intervals and does not represent duration (use gantt-schedule if you need to show duration)
State in source that future milestones are planned, not confirmed
Keep date labels to 10 characters or fewer (e.g., 2026/09), with consistent granularity

logic-tree.description: Decomposes an issue MECE-style, showing structurally where the problem (or the solution) lies
logic-tree.answers: What elements can this problem be broken down into, and which one matters most?
guardrails: tree is nested as [label, [children…]]. Each child is either the same shape or a string. Depth beyond 4, or insufficient column width, raises an error at render time
Limit to 5 leaves (to preserve the 0.46in node height). Beyond that, split the tree across two slides
MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) is not enforced by the component itself. Keep one decomposition criterion per level
Do not mix a Why tree (cause decomposition) and a How tree (solution decomposition) into a single tree
Write in insight which branch matters most, and the basis for that judgment

kpi-tree.description: Decomposes the KGI into its component metrics, showing which metric is driving the gap (or the achievement) against target
kpi-tree.answers: Which component metric is producing the gap between target and actual?
guardrails: The root is a single KGI. Write node labels as "metric name\nactual value" (or "actual / target" if showing the ratio to target)
Only use parent-child relationships explainable by arithmetic (Revenue = New + Existing, New = Leads × Conversion rate, …). Do not include elements that can't be explained this way
Every figure requires a source. State the period and aggregation definition in source
Limit to 5 leaves (to preserve the 0.46in node height for two-line labels). When there are many metrics, expand only the bottleneck branch and collapse the rest at a higher level
Write in insight which metric is the primary driver of the gap, quantified (e.g., of the -12% shortfall, -9% comes from the opportunity-conversion rate)

why-why.description: Shows the chain produced by repeatedly asking "why" from an observed event down to the root cause
why-why.answers: What is the root cause of this event, and where should we act?
guardrails: chain[0] is the observed event, and the last entry is the root cause. Don't skip steps — dig one "why" at a time
Don't stop at "the person in charge was careless" or "low awareness." Dig down to systemic and process-level factors
Word each step as something verifiable by fact. Mark any step that hasn't been verified with (hypothesis)
Limit to 6 steps due to width constraints. If the cause branches into multiple paths partway through, use fishbone-diagram instead
Write in insight the countermeasure (recurrence-prevention action) aimed at the root cause, distinguished from a symptomatic fix

fishbone-diagram.description: Lists hypothesized causes of a problem by category, to identify where to start verifying
fishbone-diagram.answers: Which category does the cause of this problem fall under, and where should verification start?
guardrails: Keep categories to a single consistent basis, such as the 4Ms (Man, Machine, Method, Material) or process names. Do not mix bases
Limit to 4 causes per category. If there are more, consolidate them or move them to a supplementary document (this diagram is not meant to prove exhaustive coverage)

What's included here are hypothesized causes. Identify the root cause via why-why or data verification; do not distinguish verified causes with bold or similar formatting (all causes are on equal footing in this diagram)
State problem as a measurable event ("monthly defect rate above 3%," not "quality is bad")
Write in insight which cause to verify next, and how

pareto-analysis.description: Overlays counts/amounts by cause with cumulative share, showing which cause to tackle first
pareto-analysis.answers: Do a small number of causes account for most of the total, and where should we start?
guardrails: Items are automatically sorted by descending value ("other" is always last). The order you pass them in carries no meaning
Use only quantities where a sum is meaningful (counts, amounts, time). Do not mix in rates or indices
State the aggregation period and sample size in source

The 80% dashed line is a rough guide. When the top causes aren't dominant (the cumulative line is close to straight), "not concentrated" is itself the finding — don't force a conclusion that focuses on the top causes
If "other" ends up the largest category, your classification is too coarse. Revisit the categories before using this chart

gap-analysis.description: Shows the current state (As-Is) and the target state (To-Be) side by side, and defines the gap to be closed
gap-analysis.answers: Where does the current state diverge from the target state, and what should we set as the issue to solve?
guardrails: As-Is must be a verified fact; To-Be must be an agreed-upon goal. If placing an unagreed aspiration into To-Be, mark it explicitly as a hypothesis in the title
List the same dimensions in the same order under asis and tobe, so the gap reads clearly row by row
Write gaps as "the issue to be closed," not as "a description of the difference" (what needs to become what state). The issue cards carry this slide's conclusion
Do not put the details of solutions (How) on this slide. Send prioritization of issues to priority-matrix
For any numeric target in To-Be, state the basis (benchmark, management target) in source

process-painpoints.description: Shows the current process flow and maps which step has which pain point
process-painpoints.answers: How does the current process flow, and which step concentrates the problems?
guardrails: steps must be the current (As-Is) flow. Do not mix in an ideal flow or the post-improvement state
Each row of pains is [step, pain point, impact]. Match the step name exactly to how it's written in steps
List only pain points verified by observation or interviews as facts. State impact in measurable terms (effort, time, money) and record the source in source
Limit to 5 rows. For a detailed flow with more than 6 steps, put it in a separate drawio-diagrams sheet and bundle the main steps here
Do not put solutions on this slide (send issue structuring to logic-tree, prioritization to priority-matrix)

pest-analysis.description: Lists macro-environment factors across Political, Economic, Social, and Technological dimensions, organizing external impacts on the business
pest-analysis.answers: What external factors are shaping our business environment?
guardrails: Include only external factors that could actually affect our business (not a general news roundup)
Distinguish facts (enacted regulations, published statistics) from expectations (under deliberation, early signs), and attach a timeframe to expectations
Do not judge opportunity vs. threat here (pass that judgment to SWOT — this slide sticks to describing the environment)
Include at least one item in each of the four quadrants. An empty quadrant reads as "not researched"
Consolidate the source of each factor in source (official gazette, statistics, research report name)

five-forces.description: Evaluates industry competitive structure through five forces (rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers)
five-forces.answers: Where does competitive pressure in this industry come from, and how strong is it?
guardrails: Write each force as "Strong / Medium / Weak: rationale" (don't give just the rating or just the rationale). title carries the conclusion — which force squeezes profitability the most
State clearly in title or source which industry (market scope) this covers. The rating changes if the scope changes
The five forces describe industry structure. Do not write our own company-specific strengths or weaknesses (send those to swot-analysis)
The rating includes the evaluator's judgment. State the source material for the rating and the evaluation date in source
The center force (industry rivalry) is also a result of the other four. This diagram does not assert causal arrows

priority-matrix.description: Plots issues on two axes — impact and ease of execution — showing where to start
priority-matrix.answers: Among the issues we've identified, which should we tackle first?
guardrails: items is [issue name, x, y]. x / y are relative values from 0 to 1 (0 = left/bottom, 1 = right/top). State the basis for the rating (impact estimate, effort estimate), the evaluator, and the evaluation date in source
Keep the issue name short enough to fit the bubble (0.8in diameter ≈ 4 characters/line). For 5 or more characters, mark the line break explicitly with \n, e.g. "Access request\nautomation"
The top-right quadrant (easy to execute × high impact) is highest priority. But since the coordinates tend to be subjective, use this to agree on relative order rather than debating exact position
Overlapping bubbles become unreadable. Limit to 8 issues, and merge issues that sit close together
Use highlight only for issues we've decided to act on (too much emphasis emphasizes nothing)
This slide does not explain the substance of each issue (what it solves). Define that in gap-analysis or logic-tree before bringing it here

claim-evidence-table.description: The standard read-alone form: claim, supporting evidence table, implication, and source, all closed on one page
guardrails: Write the title as "what can be said" in two lines or fewer; never as a caption describing the table
Keep the implication within what the table shows. Never restate the title or introduce new information
Never show a number without a source. Cut any row you cannot source

exhibit-analysis.description: Puts a chart inside a numbered exhibit frame with the reading on the right, making one page referable from the body and appendix
exhibit-analysis.answers: What can be read from this exhibit?
guardrails: The exhibit number exists for cross-reference from the body and appendix; sequential numbering is the author's responsibility
Keep the implication within what the chart shows; never add information that is not in the figure
Bar chart baselines are fixed at zero. Never exaggerate an axis to inflate a difference

exec-summary-readable.description: Situation, complication, and resolution in three tiers plus supporting points, so the first page alone enables a decision
exec-summary-readable.answers: What, in the end, is this document asking the reader to decide?
guardrails: The condition is that this one page alone enables the decision; the body serves as supporting evidence
Write the resolution tier as a conclusion with numbers; never end on "to be considered"
If the supporting points exceed five, rework the body's chapter structure instead

conclusion-rationale-implication.description: Leads with the conclusion, then rationale cards and the next action (So What), read as a one-page pyramid
conclusion-rationale-implication.answers: What is the conclusion, why does it hold, and what happens next?
guardrails: Put the conclusion in the title; never make the reader reach the end of the body to find it
Limit the rationale to 3-4 non-overlapping points; split to another slide beyond five
So What states the next action; never a restatement of the rationale or the title

dense-comparison-table.description: Compares options in a dot-rating matrix and shows the recommendation with its reasoning on one page
dense-comparison-table.answers: Which option is best, and why recommend it?
guardrails: Limit criteria to those that affect the decision; never pad with filler criteria
Always state the basis for the scoring (quotes, evaluation sessions) in the source
Write the recommendation as an overall judgment that concedes weaknesses; never disguise it as a clean sweep

key-message-storyline.description: Lines up the body's action titles in order — the horizontal logic — showing on one page that the titles alone carry the argument
key-message-storyline.answers: Does the argument hold when reading only the titles?
guardrails: Each row must match the action title of its body slide; never rewrite as a summary
If the argument breaks here, fix the structure before building the slides
Write each row as a claim ("what can be said"); never as a table-of-contents topic

faq-objection-handling.description: Pairs the objections expected at the approval meeting with sourced answers, preempting the Q&A on one page
faq-objection-handling.answers: How will we answer the expected objections?
guardrails: Every answer must carry its basis (exhibit numbers, appendix, test results)
Leave unanswerable concerns visible; a glossed-over answer destroys the document's credibility
Limit concerns to ones that will actually come up; never stage weak strawman objections

one-page-brief.description: The densest page in the pack: exhibit chart, comparison table, implication, decision items, and source, all on one approval-ready page
one-page-brief.answers: Can the approver confirm the judgment and the decision items from this one page alone?
guardrails: This page is the final check for approval. The exhibit and table summarize the body; never introduce a first-appearance number here
Write decision items so Yes/No can be said, with a deadline. "Continue considering" is not a decision item
Pack in information, not text. Keep table cells short and nominal
